paras: The lynching of Juan Monterea was the hanging of a man accused of murder by a group of men in Taos County, New Mexico Territory, on the night of Saturday, June 11, 1881. Monterea had been arrested and jailed after Leon M. Gallagher, who had objected to his treatment of his mother, was killed with a hoe. According to a Santa Fe dispatch, a "large body of men" took him from jail and hanged him from the railing of the courthouse. The story ran as a short wire item in papers across the country in the following two weeks.

According to a Santa Fe special relayed from Cincinnati on June 16, Monterea "abused his aged mother" in Taos County, and Gallagher remonstrated with him. Monterea was accused of then killing Gallagher with a hoe. A separate Santa Fe dispatch printed in the Omaha Daily Bee said Gallagher was trying to stop Monterea from beating his mother, was assaulted, and died of his injuries within a few hours.

Monterea was arrested and jailed. The Omaha Daily Bee's dispatch said public opinion was so strongly against him, both for his treatment of his mother and for the assault on Gallagher, that a large body of men took him from the jail and hanged him to the railing of the courthouse. The Cincinnati version put the lynching on Saturday night and attributed it to "the citizens", while a later roundup item said a "lynching party" hanged him "on the same evening" as the killing. One brief called the men a "mob" and another "the vigilantes"; none of the reports gives their number or names any of them.
No report of an inquest, arrests or any official response to the lynching appears in the coverage, and no New Mexico paper's account was found.

The first report, a Santa Fe dispatch dated June 16, appeared that day in the Alexandria Gazette under the headline "Murderer Lynched," with the county garbled as "Toussaint." On June 17 the Cincinnati-relayed special ran in the Savannah Morning News as "A Murderer Lynched" and in the New-York Tribune as "Murder Followed by Lynching," while other dailies carried a one-sentence brief calling Monterea "a murderer" lynched by a mob. The Omaha Daily Bee printed the fullest account under the headline "Lynch Law Ends the Life of a Murderous Mexican."

From June 22 to 25 a weekly news-roundup paragraph, saying Monterea killed "Lem Gallagher" for interfering in a fight with his mother and that a lynching party swung him from the courthouse railing, ran in country weeklies in Minnesota, Wisconsin, Indiana and elsewhere. Another brief, in the Southern Standard and Fair Play on June 25, said he "was hanged by the vigilantes." The Washington Evening Critic treated the case with irony, calling Monterea a "New Mexican rough" and writing that "the moral sense of the community was vindicated immediately" by the lynching. All the reports took the accusation against Monterea as established and none questioned the lynching; no paper described him as Black.

The papers differ on details: most place the events in Taos County, but the Evening Critic placed Gallagher "at Santa Fe." Gallagher's first name appears as "Leon M." in the Santa Fe special and as "Lem" in the roundup item, and the Omaha Daily Bee alone says he lived a few hours after the assault rather than being killed outright.

He was hanged without trial after being taken from jail by 'a large body of men' (A6), a 'lynching party' (A8), in retribution for the killing of Gallagher (A3, A6); the victim is described as Mexican, not Black (A6).

Two distinct Santa Fe dispatches, the Cincinnati-relayed special (A3, A4) and the Omaha Daily Bee's report (A6), agree on the killing of Gallagher, the arrest and the lynching; the roundup item (A8) agrees as well.

framing.detail: Headlines 'Murderer Lynched' and 'Murder Followed by Lynching' over the bare Santa Fe special; the accusation stated as fact.
Omaha Daily Bee headline 'Lynch Law Ends the Life of a Murderous Mexican' and an account explaining the lynching by public opinion against him.
The Washington Evening Critic wrote ironically that 'the moral sense of the community was vindicated immediately' by lynching 'the disrespectful Juan'.

conflicts.note: The Evening Critic's 'at Santa Fe' probably comes from the dispatch's dateline; the Santa Fe dispatches themselves place it at Taos.
